title: The full test suite never fails on unchanged code when the Mac is busy
goal: Some checks in the test suite fail now and then in a full run and pass on their own, so a runner or a release cannot trust a red run and has to run the whole suite again. One is a timing check judged against a flat number of milliseconds; three are video checks (a size estimate, a cut export, a moving title background). Each one either reads something the rest of the suite changes, or shows a real problem under load: find out which and fix it.

2026-11-09 findings: (1) The hardware H.264 encoder takes 32 sessions across the whole Mac (VTCompressionSession probe: 32 hardware, the rest software with no error; one process holding 24 left another 8). A writer past that silently gets the software encoder, which ignores the budget: a 2 s Small document landed 1,887,382 bytes vs 234,015 (new HardwareEncoderTests reproduces it). That is the busy-size failure. Fixed in the app: writers ask for the hardware encoder and wait up to 30 s for a session (HardwareEncoder.swift), then fall back. (2) Test bug: VideoExportBudgetTests.bytes(of:) read url.resourceValues, which caches the size on the URL, so BusyVideoSizeTests' lightest-of-three re-read the first write's size every go (three goes read 2,439,432 while the files were 2,439,432 / 2,684,923 / 1,955,784). (3) Test bug: BusyVideoSizeTests and VideoExportBudgetTests run at once in the serialized process and both wrote busy-3s.mp4, busy-4s.mp4, busy-sound-4s.mp4, tone-4s.m4a in one shared folder. (4) dragTheWidth, the Aurora/Glass page budget and the live-backdrop budget moved into ...PerfTests suites judged by MachineSpeed.checkFrames against the 1080p frame ruler. Ruled out for the 30 s reader stall: encoder cap (export with 32 sessions held took 0.2 s), dispatch pool starvation (70 blocked global threads: 0.17 s; the 30 s timer itself runs on that pool and did fire in the real failures).

Chart budget reproduced 2026-11-09: 16 bounded perl spinners, AnimatedChartPerfTests read Donut 19.2 ms vs bound 18.5 (frame ruler 4.3 against 3.3, 1.3x) and failed 1 of 3. A from-scratch release or debug compile alone did not reproduce it (load 4 to 12). Fixed with a CPU yardstick (MachineSpeed .cpu, baseline 3.3 ms, busiestFactor): under the same load the CPU ruler read 6.6 to 7.0 and 5 of 5 passed; all 33 stopwatch tests in 16 suites passed under 16 spinners.

Reader stall: caught once with the diagnostic patch in an UNLOADED full run (run 5): the stalled read answered by itself after 59.7 s; the VTDecoderXPCService serving it was idle with its AVDFrameReceiver waiting on the hardware, and a media thread in the test process sat in RemoteVideoDecoder_DecodeFrameWithOptions (WaitOnConditionTimed). So: a hardware decode that never comes back until the system's own ~60 s timeout. Not reproducible on demand: 4 runs beside a release build, 5 loops of the video suites beside 4 GPU burners and up to 8 concurrent media test processes caught none. Chose to start the picture pass again once on a fresh reader (new decoder session) over raising the 30 s limit to 90 s, because a lost frame costs the person 30 s instead of the export, and a decoder stuck for good is still reported after the second go.

Also found and fixed: GuardedReads' 30 s give-up clock ran on DispatchQueue.global, so with 90 global threads blocked an export parked for good (probe: 40/56/62/66/72 blocked read in 0.1 s, 90 parked the whole run). The clock has its own queue; GuardedReadsTests 'A stuck read is still given up on when every ordinary background thread is taken' failed at 10.7 s before, passes in 0.2 s after.

left rough: OffThePool runs blocking decodes on the capped global pool too (not the cause here, the stalled process had about 50 threads; a person would only notice if dozens of decodes ran at once). PieceCopyWriterTests failed notCopyable in every process with 8 media test processes at once (artificial; never seen in a full run). Neither filed.
